# Herdr compatibility

<!-- Generated by tools/render_compatibility.py. Edit the gates it reads, not this file. -->

Which Herdr releases this revision of Tether was exercised against, so it can be
checked before installing rather than inferred from a version requirement. At a
release tag this file is that release's record; on `main` it describes `main`.

## Exercised

| Platform | Herdr release | How it was exercised |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ubuntu 24.04 | 0.8.0 | Official release asset, verified by SHA-256, then the live product smoke |
| macOS 14 | 0.8.0 | Official release asset, verified by SHA-256, then the live product smoke |

Every row is a real run: the gate downloads the official Herdr release asset for
the runner's platform, verifies it against a pinned SHA-256, validates the
socket API schema it reports, builds Tether from the locked manifest, and drives
a workload through `tmux` end to end. A row names the runner image the gate
uses, not every architecture of that operating system, and a row exists only for
a platform the gate actually covers.

## Socket protocol

Tether speaks Herdr's socket API from protocol 19, which Herdr 0.8.0 ships. Its
checks audit through protocol 20; that ceiling comes from reviewing newer
upstream Herdr rather than from the releases in the table above, so it says what
Tether has been read against, not what it was run against.

A Herdr reporting a protocol above 20 is not refused: `herdr-tether doctor`
reports it as newer and not yet verified, and Tether keeps working with the
parts of the API it knows. A Herdr below protocol 19 is not used: Mission
Control reports the upgrade it needs, and the Observer paths report Herdr as not
connected rather than explaining why.

## What this does not claim

Herdr releases other than 0.8.0 are not covered here. Tether may work with them,
and its protocol floor is the real compatibility boundary at runtime, but this
table says only what was exercised.

Unreleased upstream Herdr is exercised separately, on a schedule, against
whatever `master` resolves to at the time. That canary is advisory: a moving
revision is not something a user can install, so it contributes no row here. It
is what the audited protocol ceiling above is read against.
